notes:
1. Maratha Empire — Overview

  • The Maratha state emerged in the western Deccan during the seventeenth century.
  • Shivaji transformed a regional power base into an independent kingdom.
  • After Shivaji, Maratha influence expanded across large parts of India.
  • During the eighteenth century, political leadership increasingly shifted from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Founder of Independent Maratha Kingdom → Shivaji

2. Geographical Base of Maratha Power

Early Maratha power developed mainly in present-day:

  • Maharashtra.
  • Western Ghats.
  • Konkan coast.
  • Deccan plateau.

3. Importance of the Western Ghats

The Western Ghats helped the Marathas because of:

  • Rugged terrain.
  • Hill forts.
  • Narrow passes.
  • Forest cover.
  • Knowledge of local routes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maratha Military Strength → Forts + Western Ghats Terrain

4. Maratha Country

The traditional Maratha homeland included:

  • Maharashtra plateau.
  • Sahyadri ranges.
  • Konkan.
  • Pune region.
  • Satara region.

5. Bhonsle Family

  • Shivaji belonged to the Bhonsle family.
  • His father was Shahaji Bhonsle.
  • His mother was Jijabai.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shivaji → Shahaji + Jijabai

6. Shahaji Bhonsle

  • Shahaji was an important military commander in the Deccan.
  • He served different Deccan powers at various stages.
  • He was associated especially with:
  • Ahmadnagar.
  • Bijapur.
  • He also held territories in the Karnataka region.

7. Jijabai

  • Jijabai played an important role in Shivaji's upbringing.
  • She was deeply associated with his early political and cultural formation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shivaji's Mother → Jijabai

8. Shivaji's Birth

  • Shivaji was born at Shivneri Fort near Junnar.
  • The widely commemorated date is 19 February 1630.
  • Older historical works sometimes gave a different chronology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shivaji → Shivneri Fort

9. Shivneri Fort

  • Shivneri is located near Junnar in Maharashtra.
  • It is one of the most important places associated with Shivaji's early life.

10. Pune Region

  • Pune became the main early political base of Shivaji.
  • The surrounding Maval region supplied important military manpower.

11. Mavals

  • Mavals are valleys and hill regions west of Pune.
  • The inhabitants of this region became important supporters and soldiers of Shivaji.
📌 Must-Memorise

Maval → Early Military Base of Shivaji

12. Dadoji Kondadev

  • Dadoji Kondadev was associated with the administration of Shahaji's Pune jagir during Shivaji's youth.
  • Older narratives credited him heavily with Shivaji's training.
  • Modern historians treat the extent of that role more cautiously.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Dadoji Kondadev → Pune Administration; Exact Role in Shivaji's Training Is Debated

13. Early Fort Policy

Shivaji understood that control of forts meant control over:

  • Mountain routes.
  • Revenue areas.
  • Military communications.
  • Local administration.

14. Torna Fort

  • Torna was one of the earliest important forts captured by Shivaji.
  • It was taken around 1646.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Major Fort Captured by Shivaji → Torna

15. Rajgad

  • Shivaji developed Rajgad as an important early capital.
  • It remained a major political centre before Raigad became the royal capital.

16. Kondana

  • Kondana Fort near Pune became an important point of conflict.
  • It was later renamed Sinhagad.

17. Purandar Fort

  • Purandar was strategically important near Pune.
  • It later became famous for the Treaty of Purandar of 1665.

18. Shivaji and Bijapur

  • Shivaji's early territorial expansion largely took place at the expense of the Bijapur Sultanate.
  • Bijapur was ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty.
📌 Must-Memorise

Early Shivaji Expansion → Against Bijapur Adil Shahis

19. Afzal Khan

  • Bijapur sent Afzal Khan to suppress Shivaji.
  • The two met near Pratapgad in 1659.
📌 Must-Memorise

Afzal Khan Episode → 1659 → Pratapgad

20. Meeting at Pratapgad

  • Shivaji and Afzal Khan met under agreed conditions.
  • The meeting turned violent.
  • Afzal Khan was killed.

21. Wagh Nakh

  • Shivaji is traditionally associated with using a weapon called the wagh nakh during the encounter.
  • Wagh nakh means tiger claws.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wagh Nakh → Shivaji–Afzal Khan Episode

22. Pratapgad Victory

  • The death of Afzal Khan was followed by a major Maratha victory over Bijapur forces.
  • Shivaji's prestige and territorial position increased sharply.

23. Panhala Fort

  • Panhala became another major Maratha-Bijapur conflict centre.
  • Shivaji was besieged there by Bijapur forces.

24. Baji Prabhu Deshpande

  • Baji Prabhu Deshpande is famous for protecting Shivaji's retreat from Panhala.
  • He fought at a mountain pass later remembered as Pavan Khind.
📌 Must-Memorise

Baji Prabhu Deshpande → Pavan Khind

25. Pavan Khind

  • Pavan Khind lies in the Western Ghats.
  • Baji Prabhu and his men delayed enemy forces while Shivaji reached safety.

26. Shivaji and the Mughals

  • Mughal-Maratha conflict intensified during Aurangzeb's reign.
  • Mughal control in the Deccan directly threatened Maratha expansion.

27. Shaista Khan

  • Aurangzeb sent Shaista Khan to suppress Shivaji.
  • Shaista Khan occupied Pune and operated from the region for several years.

28. Pune Attack of 1663

  • Shivaji launched a surprise night attack on Shaista Khan's residence in Pune in 1663.
  • Shaista Khan escaped but was injured.
  • The raid became one of Shivaji's most famous military exploits.
📌 Must-Memorise

1663 → Shivaji's Surprise Attack on Shaista Khan

29. Surat Raid

  • Shivaji raided Surat in 1664.
  • Surat was one of the richest Mughal commercial ports.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Major Surat Raid → 1664

30. Importance of Surat

Surat was important for:

  • Red Sea trade.
  • Persian Gulf trade.
  • European companies.
  • Pilgrimage traffic.
  • Mughal customs revenue.

31. Raja Jai Singh I

  • Aurangzeb sent the Rajput commander Raja Jai Singh I of Amber against Shivaji.
  • Jai Singh conducted a systematic military campaign.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jai Singh → Mughal Commander Against Shivaji

32. Siege of Purandar

  • Mughal forces besieged Purandar in 1665.
  • Murarbaji Deshpande became famous for his defence of the fort.

33. Treaty of Purandar

  • Treaty of Purandar was concluded in 1665.
  • It was negotiated between:
  • Shivaji.
  • Raja Jai Singh I.
📌 Must-Memorise

1665 → Treaty of Purandar → Shivaji + Jai Singh

34. Main Effect of Treaty of Purandar

  • Shivaji agreed to surrender several forts to the Mughals.
  • He retained a smaller group of forts.
  • His son Sambhaji was to receive Mughal rank.

35. Shivaji's Visit to Agra

  • Shivaji visited Aurangzeb's court at Agra in 1666.
  • He expected honourable treatment after the Purandar settlement.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shivaji at Agra → 1666

36. Agra Incident

  • Shivaji was dissatisfied with his treatment at the Mughal court.
  • He was placed under restricted supervision.

37. Escape from Agra

  • Shivaji escaped from confinement in 1666.
  • Popular tradition describes concealment involving baskets, although details vary in historical accounts.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Agra Escape → Certain; Exact Basket Story Is Traditional

38. Renewal of Maratha Expansion

  • After returning to the Deccan, Shivaji gradually resumed expansion.
  • Many forts surrendered earlier to the Mughals were recovered.

39. Sinhagad

  • Kondana Fort was recaptured by Maratha forces in 1670.
  • The battle is strongly associated with Tanaji Malusare.
📌 Must-Memorise

1670 → Kondana/Sinhagad → Tanaji Malusare

40. Tanaji Malusare

  • Tanaji Malusare was a close associate of Shivaji.
  • He died during the capture of Kondana Fort.

41. Sinhagad Name

  • Kondana later became widely known as Sinhagad, meaning Lion's Fort.
  • Popular tradition connects the name with Tanaji's bravery.

42. Second Raid on Surat

  • Shivaji again raided Surat in 1670.
  • This demonstrated continuing Maratha offensive capacity.

43. Raigad

  • Raigad became Shivaji's principal royal capital.
  • His coronation was held there.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shivaji's Capital at Coronation → Raigad

44. Coronation of Shivaji

  • Shivaji was formally crowned at Raigad in 1674.
  • He assumed the title Chhatrapati.
📌 Must-Memorise

1674 → Shivaji's Coronation → Raigad → Chhatrapati

45. Gaga Bhatt

  • Gaga Bhatt, a Brahmana scholar from Varanasi, officiated at Shivaji's coronation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gaga Bhatt → Shivaji's Coronation

46. Chhatrapati

  • Chhatrapati became the royal title associated with the Maratha sovereign.
  • It symbolised independent kingship.

47. Hindavi Swarajya

  • The expression Hindavi Swarajya is associated with Shivaji's political vision in Maratha tradition.
  • It broadly conveys indigenous or self-rule.
  • The phrase should not be mechanically equated with modern nationalism.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Hindavi Swarajya → Early Modern Political Idea, Not Modern Nation-State Concept

48. Shivaji's Southern Campaign

  • Shivaji launched an important southern expedition during 1676–1678.
  • His forces entered parts of:
  • Karnataka.
  • Tamil region.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Shivaji → Southern Campaign → Gingee and Vellore Region

49. Gingee

  • Gingee Fort in present-day Tamil Nadu came under Maratha control during Shivaji's southern campaign.
  • It later became extremely important under Rajaram.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Gingee → Shivaji + Later Rajaram

50. Vellore

  • Shivaji's southern campaign also extended toward the Vellore region.
  • Control of forts was central to his southern strategy.

51. Shahaji's Southern Connections

  • Shivaji's father Shahaji had earlier possessed important interests in the Karnataka region.
  • This gave the Bhonsle family political connections in southern India.

52. Ekoji / Venkoji

  • Ekoji, also called Venkoji, was Shivaji's half-brother.
  • He became the founder of the Maratha dynasty of Thanjavur.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Ekoji / Venkoji → Shivaji's Half-Brother → Thanjavur Maratha Dynasty

53. Shivaji's Administration

Shivaji developed a disciplined administrative system covering:

  • Central administration.
  • Revenue.
  • Military.
  • Forts.
  • Justice.
  • Religious grants.

54. Ashtapradhan

  • Shivaji's council of eight principal ministers was called Ashtapradhan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ashtapradhan → Council of Eight

55. Peshwa

  • Peshwa was the chief minister.
  • He supervised general administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Peshwa → Prime Minister

56. Amatya / Mazumdar

  • Amatya was responsible mainly for:
  • Finance.
  • Accounts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amatya → Finance

57. Sachiv

  • Sachiv was associated with:
  • Official correspondence.
  • Royal documents.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sachiv → Correspondence

58. Mantri

  • Mantri maintained:
  • Court records.
  • Daily chronicles.
  • Intelligence-related information.

59. Senapati

  • Senapati was commander-in-chief.
📌 Must-Memorise

Senapati → Army

60. Sumant / Dabir

  • Sumant or Dabir handled:
  • Foreign relations.
  • Diplomatic correspondence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sumant → Foreign Affairs

61. Nyayadhish

  • Nyayadhish was chief judicial authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nyayadhish → Justice

62. Panditrao

  • Panditrao supervised:
  • Religious matters.
  • Charitable grants.
  • Religious institutions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Panditrao → Religious Grants

63. Ashtapradhan — Memory Chain

  • Peshwa → General administration.
  • Amatya → Finance.
  • Sachiv → Correspondence.
  • Mantri → Records/intelligence.
  • Senapati → Military.
  • Sumant → Foreign affairs.
  • Nyayadhish → Justice.
  • Panditrao → Religious affairs.

64. Nature of Ashtapradhan

  • Ministers advised the king.
  • Ultimate authority remained with Shivaji.
  • Offices were not originally intended to function as independent hereditary centres of power.

65. Provincial Administration

  • Shivaji divided territory into administrative units.
  • Local officials supervised:
  • Revenue.
  • Military order.
  • Village administration.

66. Village Administration

The village remained an important administrative unit.

Important officials included:

  • Patil.
  • Kulkarni.

67. Patil

  • Patil was generally the village headman.
📌 Must-Memorise

Patil → Village Head

68. Kulkarni

  • Kulkarni maintained village accounts and records.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kulkarni → Village Accountant

69. Deshmukh

  • Deshmukhs were influential hereditary local revenue and landed intermediaries.
  • Shivaji attempted to restrict excessive independent power of such local elites.

70. Deshpande

  • Deshpandes were associated with district-level revenue accounts and records.

71. Shivaji's Revenue Administration

  • Shivaji sought direct assessment of agricultural land.
  • Revenue assessment was based on:
  • Measurement.
  • Productivity.
  • Crop conditions.

72. Land Revenue

  • Land revenue formed the principal regular source of state income.
  • The assessment varied according to productivity and local conditions.

73. Chauth

  • Chauth literally means one-fourth.
  • It referred to a levy equivalent to 25% of assessed revenue collected from territories outside direct Maratha administration in return for non-attack or protection.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chauth → 25%

74. Sardeshmukhi

  • Sardeshmukhi was an additional levy traditionally calculated at 10%.
  • Marathas claimed it on the basis of superior regional rights.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sardeshmukhi → 10%

75. Chauth vs Sardeshmukhi

  • Chauth → 25%.
  • Sardeshmukhi → Additional 10%.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

Chauth ≠ Sardeshmukhi

76. Importance of Revenue System

Revenue financed:

  • Forts.
  • Cavalry.
  • Infantry.
  • Administration.
  • Naval forces.

77. Maratha Military System

Shivaji's forces included:

  • Cavalry.
  • Infantry.
  • Fort garrisons.
  • Navy.

78. Cavalry

Two important categories commonly discussed were:

  • Bargirs.
  • Silahdars.

79. Bargir

  • Bargirs were cavalrymen provided with horses and equipment by the state.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bargir → State-Supplied Horse

80. Silahdar

  • Silahdars supplied their own:
  • Horses.
  • Weapons.
  • Equipment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Silahdar → Own Horse and Equipment

81. Ganimi Kava

  • Shivaji used highly mobile warfare suited to rugged terrain.
  • Maratha tradition refers to such methods as Ganimi Kava.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ganimi Kava → Maratha Guerrilla-Style Warfare

82. Features of Maratha Warfare

Important features included:

  • Surprise attacks.
  • Rapid cavalry movement.
  • Intelligence.
  • Avoiding unnecessary pitched battles.
  • Fort networks.
  • Attacks on enemy supply lines.

83. Forts

Forts were central to Maratha defence.

Types included:

  • Hill forts.
  • Land forts.
  • Sea forts.

84. Important Shivaji Forts

Important forts included:

  • Raigad.
  • Rajgad.
  • Torna.
  • Pratapgad.
  • Sinhagad.
  • Purandar.
  • Panhala.
  • Sindhudurg.

85. Fort Administration

  • Major forts had separate officials responsible for:
  • Military security.
  • Stores.
  • Accounts.
  • This reduced the danger of one officer monopolising control.

86. Maratha Navy

  • Shivaji recognised the strategic importance of naval power.
  • His navy was used to protect:
  • Konkan coast.
  • Maritime trade.
  • Coastal forts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shivaji → Developed Strong Maratha Naval Policy

87. Sindhudurg

  • Sindhudurg was a major sea fort constructed under Shivaji.
  • It lies off the Malvan coast.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sindhudurg → Shivaji → Sea Fort

88. Vijaydurg

  • Vijaydurg became another important Maratha naval base on the Konkan coast.

89. Naval Enemies

Maratha naval interests brought conflict or rivalry with:

  • Siddis of Janjira.
  • Portuguese.
  • English.
  • Other coastal powers.

90. Janjira

  • Janjira was a powerful island fortress controlled by the Siddis.
  • Shivaji was unable to permanently capture it.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Janjira → Siddi Stronghold, Not Permanently Captured by Shivaji

91. Religious Policy of Shivaji

  • Shivaji was personally Hindu and patronised Hindu institutions.
  • His administration also employed Muslims.
  • He generally avoided indiscriminate religious destruction as a governing principle.

92. Shivaji and Mosques

  • Contemporary and later accounts record orders protecting religious establishments in various contexts.
  • His political conflicts were primarily territorial and military.

93. Shivaji and Women

  • Maratha traditions strongly emphasise Shivaji's orders against molestation of women during military campaigns.
  • Discipline over troops contributed to his political reputation.

94. Language of Administration

  • Marathi was extensively used in administration.
  • Persian administrative terminology also remained influential.

95. Rajyavyavahara Kosha

  • Rajyavyavahara Kosha was compiled to provide Sanskritised/Marathi alternatives for Persian administrative terminology.
  • It is associated with Shivaji's period.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rajyavyavahara Kosha → Administrative Vocabulary → Shivaji

96. Shivaji's Death

  • Shivaji died at Raigad in 1680.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shivaji → Died 1680 → Raigad

97. Succession After Shivaji

A struggle developed involving:

  • Sambhaji.
  • Rajaram.
  • Court factions.

Sambhaji ultimately secured the throne.

98. Sambhaji

  • Sambhaji was Shivaji's eldest son.
  • He became Chhatrapati after Shivaji's death.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shivaji → Sambhaji

99. Sambhaji's Reign

  • Sambhaji ruled during intense conflict with Aurangzeb.
  • He continued resistance against Mughal expansion in the Deccan.

100. Sambhaji and Portuguese

  • Sambhaji also fought against Portuguese interests along the western coast.

101. Capture of Sambhaji

  • Sambhaji was captured by Mughal forces at Sangameshwar in 1689.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sambhaji Captured → Sangameshwar → 1689

102. Death of Sambhaji

  • Sambhaji was executed on Aurangzeb's orders in 1689.
  • His death did not end Maratha resistance.

103. Rajaram

  • Rajaram was Shivaji's younger son.
  • He became Chhatrapati after Sambhaji's death.
📌 Must-Memorise

After Sambhaji → Rajaram

104. Rajaram's Move to Gingee

  • Rajaram escaped Mughal pressure in Maharashtra.
  • He travelled to Gingee in Tamil Nadu.
  • Gingee became a major Maratha resistance headquarters.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Rajaram → Gingee → Maratha Resistance

105. Why Gingee Was Important

Gingee was:

  • Strongly fortified.
  • Far from the main Mughal base.
  • Located in difficult terrain.
  • Strategically placed in South India.

106. Mughal Siege of Gingee

  • Mughal commander Zulfiqar Khan led a prolonged siege of Gingee.
  • The siege continued for several years.

107. Capture of Gingee

  • Mughal forces finally captured Gingee in 1698.
  • Rajaram had escaped before the fort fell.
📌 Must-Memorise

1698 → Gingee Captured by Zulfiqar Khan

108. Return of Rajaram

  • Rajaram returned to Maharashtra.
  • He continued resistance from western India.

109. Death of Rajaram

  • Rajaram died in 1700.

110. Tarabai

  • Tarabai was Rajaram's widow.
  • She became one of the most capable leaders of Maratha resistance after his death.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tarabai → Led Resistance After Rajaram

111. Tarabai's Leadership

  • Tarabai acted as regent for her young son Shivaji II.
  • She coordinated Maratha operations against Mughal forces.

112. Aurangzeb's Final Years

  • Aurangzeb spent much of his final decades campaigning against the Marathas.
  • Despite capturing many forts, Mughal forces could not permanently destroy Maratha resistance.

113. Aurangzeb's Death

  • Aurangzeb died in 1707.
  • His death dramatically altered the political balance in the Deccan.

114. Shahu

  • Shahu was the son of Sambhaji.
  • He had been held in Mughal captivity.
  • He was released after Aurangzeb's death.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shahu → Son of Sambhaji

115. Shahu vs Tarabai

  • Shahu claimed the Maratha throne.
  • Tarabai opposed his claim on behalf of her own line.

116. Battle of Khed

  • Shahu defeated Tarabai's forces at the Battle of Khed in 1707.
  • He established his principal authority at Satara.
📌 Must-Memorise

1707 → Battle of Khed → Shahu's Ascendancy

117. Satara and Kolhapur

  • The dynastic conflict eventually contributed to separate Maratha royal lines centred at:
  • Satara.
  • Kolhapur.

118. Rise of the Peshwas

  • Under Shahu, the office of Peshwa became increasingly powerful.
  • Political leadership gradually shifted from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa.
📌 Must-Memorise

18th-Century Maratha Power → Rise of Peshwas

119. Balaji Vishwanath

  • Balaji Vishwanath became Peshwa under Shahu in 1713.
  • He is regarded as the founder of the powerful hereditary Peshwa line.
📌 Must-Memorise

Balaji Vishwanath → Peshwa → 1713

120. Importance of Balaji Vishwanath

He:

  • Strengthened Shahu.
  • Reconciled important Maratha chiefs.
  • Negotiated with Mughal political factions.
  • Expanded Maratha revenue claims.

121. Sayyid Brothers and Marathas

  • Balaji Vishwanath allied with the Sayyid Brothers during Mughal political struggles.
  • Maratha forces participated in events at Delhi.

122. Mughal Recognition of Maratha Claims

  • Agreements during this period recognised Maratha claims to collect:
  • Chauth.
  • Sardeshmukhi.
  • These claims related especially to Deccan territories.

123. Balaji Vishwanath's Death

  • Balaji Vishwanath died in 1720.

124. Baji Rao I

  • Baji Rao I succeeded his father Balaji Vishwanath as Peshwa in 1720.
  • He was one of the greatest Maratha military commanders.
📌 Must-Memorise

Baji Rao I → Peshwa 1720–1740

125. Baji Rao's Political Objective

  • Baji Rao sought rapid Maratha expansion into northern and central India.
  • He exploited the weakening Mughal Empire.

126. Baji Rao's Cavalry Warfare

  • Baji Rao relied heavily on:
  • Speed.
  • Mobile cavalry.
  • Surprise.
  • Strategic manoeuvre.

127. Battle of Palkhed

  • Battle of Palkhed was fought in 1728.
  • Baji Rao I defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad.
📌 Must-Memorise

1728 → Palkhed → Baji Rao I Defeated Nizam

128. Importance of Palkhed

  • Baji Rao avoided a costly direct assault.
  • He used superior manoeuvre to cut the Nizam's communications and supplies.
  • The battle is regarded as a classic example of mobile warfare.

129. Nizam-ul-Mulk

  • Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah founded the autonomous Hyderabad state.
  • He was a major rival of expanding Maratha power.

130. Bundelkhand

  • Baji Rao assisted Bundela ruler Chhatrasal against Muhammad Khan Bangash.
  • Chhatrasal rewarded the Marathas with territorial rights.
📌 Must-Memorise

Baji Rao I → Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand

131. Mastani

  • Mastani is traditionally associated with Baji Rao I.
  • She was connected with Chhatrasal's family and became an important figure in later popular tradition.

132. Malwa

  • Under Baji Rao I, Maratha power expanded substantially into Malwa.
  • This provided a gateway into northern India.

133. Baji Rao's Delhi Campaign

  • In 1737, Baji Rao rapidly advanced toward Delhi.
  • The campaign demonstrated Mughal inability to prevent Maratha penetration into the imperial heartland.
📌 Must-Memorise

1737 → Baji Rao's Rapid Advance to Delhi

134. Battle / Convention of Bhopal

  • Maratha forces outmanoeuvred the Nizam near Bhopal in 1737–38.
  • The resulting settlement strengthened Maratha claims in Malwa.

135. Chimaji Appa

  • Chimaji Appa was Baji Rao I's brother.
  • He led major campaigns against the Portuguese on India's west coast.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chimaji Appa → Portuguese Wars

136. Capture of Vasai / Bassein

  • Chimaji Appa captured the Portuguese stronghold of Bassein in 1739.
📌 Must-Memorise

1739 → Bassein/Vasai → Chimaji Appa Defeated Portuguese

137. Death of Baji Rao I

  • Baji Rao I died in 1740 at Raverkhedi near the Narmada.

138. Balaji Baji Rao

  • Balaji Baji Rao succeeded Baji Rao I as Peshwa.
  • He is popularly known as Nana Saheb.
📌 Must-Memorise

Balaji Baji Rao → Nana Saheb → Peshwa 1740–1761

139. Maratha Expansion Under Nana Saheb

Maratha influence expanded into:

  • Malwa.
  • Gujarat.
  • Bundelkhand.
  • Delhi.
  • Punjab.
  • Eastern India.

140. Maratha Confederacy

  • During the eighteenth century, powerful Maratha chiefs developed semi-autonomous spheres.
  • Together they formed what is commonly called the Maratha Confederacy.

141. Major Maratha Houses

Important houses included:

  • Peshwa → Pune.
  • Scindia/Shinde → Gwalior.
  • Holkar → Indore.
  • Gaekwad → Baroda.
  • Bhonsle → Nagpur.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pune–Peshwa

Gwalior–Scindia

Indore–Holkar

Baroda–Gaekwad

Nagpur–Bhonsle

142. Scindia / Shinde

  • The Scindia family became powerful in:
  • Malwa.
  • Gwalior.
